The cross-GPU price movement observed during the week of August 17–23 reveals a pattern worth examining closely. AIMC's data shows that out of 8,138 observations across 35 marketplaces, upward price movement was concentrated at the two ends of the performance spectrum: the newest frontier hardware and older consumer-grade silicon moved in tandem, while mid-tier workhorses held flat. The B300 SXM led all movers at +2.0% ($7.50 to $7.65), the B200 SXM followed at +1.0% ($6.11 to $6.17), and simultaneously the RTX 3090 ticked up +0.7% ($0.44 to $0.45) and the RTX A4000 gained the same +0.7% ($0.27 to $0.28). Against this, the H100 SXM and H200 SXM both closed the week completely flat. That divergence — frontier and budget moving, mid-tier stationary — is a pattern the data surfaces but does not fully explain.

One interpretation consistent with what we observe is that demand pressure is bifurcating: buyers seeking maximum throughput are absorbing the incremental cost increases on Blackwell-generation hardware, while a separate, more price-sensitive segment is filling capacity with whatever is cheapest. Our weekly observations indicate the L40S, available across 14 marketplaces with a median price range of $0.63 to $2.48 per GPU-hour, gained only $0.01 on the week, suggesting that mid-tier inference and fine-tuning workloads are not experiencing the same demand pull. With a single week of data, however, we cannot distinguish a structural demand bifurcation from normal week-to-week price noise across 113 distinct SKUs.

results.title: Truist Raises CoreWeave Price Target to $165, Citing Pricing Power Over Rising GPU Costs · TechEchelon
highlights:
Truist Securities raised its CoreWeave price target to $165 from $155, implying nearly 88% upside, arguing the cloud infrastructure company's 25% July price hike more than offsets Nvidia's reported GPU cost increases of more than 15%.

...

Truist Securities reiterated its buy rating on CoreWeave on Monday and lifted its price target on the cloud infrastructure company to $165 per share from $155, implying nearly 88% upside from Friday's closing price, as the firm argued the company's ability to raise its own prices more than offsets surging GPU costs.

The call comes amid a broader industry reckoning over the cost of Nvidia's latest graphics processors. Nvidia has reportedly raised prices on its newest GPUs by more than 15%, a move that analysts say has threatened to compress CoreWeave's margins — the company purchases GPUs from Nvidia and other chipmakers, then rents out that compute capacity to cloud customers.

CoreWeave responded in July by hiking prices across its inventory by 25%, according to Truist analyst Arvind Ramnani, who argued that move has given the company meaningful insulation from the cost pressure.

"Pricing power [is] more than offsetting rising GPU costs," Ramnani said in a note to clients Monday. "We expect CRWV's higher pricing to largely flow through to margins in 2H26 as NVIDIA's increases are expected to affect systems shipped early next year."

Ramnani's analysis projects that contribution margins on future longer-duration contracts could expand from approximately 24% to roughly 33%. He added that shorter-duration deals and the re-contracting of prior-generation GPUs could generate additional upside, noting that only Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems are affected by Nvidia's price increases.

results.title: OVHcloud raises prices due to AI demand | iMasters
highlights:
The price hike of up to 87% on OVHcloud servers exposes how GPU memory demand is repricing infrastructure for those who don't even come close to running AI models.

OVHcloud will raise prices across much of its catalog this fall (Northern Hemisphere), and the cause isn't in the products that will get more expensive. According to an InfoQ report, founder Octave Klaba attributes the move to the accelerated buildout of AI infrastructure, which is pulling manufacturing capacity away from the components any ordinary server is built with.

...

The numbers come from OVHcloud's own purchasing. Indexing June 2025 as base 100, memory reached 604 by June 2026, SSDs hit 323, and HDDs hit 148. In other words: the company now pays roughly 6x the RAM price it paid a year ago. And the forecast gets worse:

> This month, June 2026, we're paying 6x the RAM price we paid in June 2025. We already know it will be 9x in September 2026, while forecasts for early 2027 stand at 12x!?

...

The increase isn't uniform. Customers renting the 2026-edition gaming servers face the steepest hike, 87%, while other recent servers rise between 40% and 59%, all effective from September. Customers on 2024-generation hardware see smaller increases upon renewal, which Klaba estimates to be three to six times lower than on a new order. Older lines, including Kimsufi, Rise, and earlier generations of Advance and Scale, are left out, as they already were in an April price increase.

Some charges are being restructured, not just raised. Starting October 1st, storage and IP addresses become separate line items on Gen3 instances, at €0.000146 per GB per hour and €0.0027 per hour. OVHcloud is also dropping the 1-, 6-, and 24-month savings plans, keeping only the 12- and 36-month options, which lock in the price for the contract's duration, a clear sign that the company is betting on cost predictability as a selling point.
